questions.prompt: A backend HTTPS probe receives HTTP 302 redirecting to a login page. TCP connectivity works. Why is the probe unhealthy?

options.text: The HTTP/HTTPS probe needs HTTP 200 rather than a redirect.
options.explanation: A non-200 response marks the HTTP health check down.

options.text: HTTPS probes only accept UDP responses.
Any response proves health, so the frontend IP must be wrong.
options.explanation: The response code is part of the health decision.

options.text: A public backend IP is required for HTTPS probes.
options.explanation: Probes can reach private backend addresses.

questions.prompt: Which NSG source service tag identifies Azure Load Balancer health-probe traffic?

options.explanation: That is not the specific probe source tag.
This tag identifies the platform health-probe source.
Traffic Manager probing is a different service.
That identifies storage service addresses rather than Load Balancer probes.

questions.prompt: Load Balancer probes are healthy, but HTTPS clients cannot connect. The probe uses TCP 9000 while the rule sends clients to TCP 443. What is a valid next check?

options.text: Assume 9000 health proves 443 is permitted and listening.
options.explanation: Different ports can have different listeners and filters.

options.text: Remove the backend pool because probing succeeded.
options.explanation: Pool removal would break distribution rather than diagnose the client path.

options.text: Inspect TCP 443 rule mapping, NSGs, guest firewall, and listener.
options.explanation: A separate probe port does not establish the application's path.

options.text: Change the DNS TTL to make the probe test TCP 443.
options.explanation: DNS TTL does not change probe or backend ports.
